subject: math
cluster: Draw, construct, and describe geometrical figures and describe the relationships between them
skillName: Drawing Geometric Shapes with Given Conditions
intro: These problems require multi-step reasoning. You may need to find a missing angle before classifying, analyze the ambiguous SSA case, determine the full range of values for an unknown side, or count and justify how many distinct triangles satisfy a set of conditions. Recall: a triangle exists from three sides only when the two shorter sides sum to more than the longest side, the interior angles must total $180^\circ$, and for a known two sides the third side must satisfy $|a-b| < c < a+b$.

items.prompt: A triangle has two sides of length $a = 7\text{ cm}$ and $b = 10\text{ cm}$. Find the full range of possible lengths for the third side $c$.

steps: The third side must satisfy the triangle inequality on both ends: $|a - b| < c < a + b$.
Compute the lower bound: $|7 - 10| = 3$, so $c > 3\text{ cm}$.
Compute the upper bound: $7 + 10 = 17$, so $c < 17\text{ cm}$.
Therefore $3\text{ cm} < c < 17\text{ cm}$. The endpoints $3$ and $17$ are excluded because they would collapse the triangle into a straight segment.

items.prompt: Two interior angles of a triangle measure $43^\circ$ and $58^\circ$. Find the third angle, then classify the triangle by its angles (acute, right, or obtuse).
items.answer: Third angle $= 79^\circ$; the triangle is acute.

steps: The three interior angles sum to $180^\circ$.
Third angle $= 180^\circ - 43^\circ - 58^\circ = 180^\circ - 101^\circ = 79^\circ$.
All three angles ($43^\circ$, $58^\circ$, $79^\circ$) are less than $90^\circ$.
Since every angle is acute, the triangle is an acute triangle.

items.prompt: In triangle $ABC$, you are given side $a = 6\text{ cm}$, side $b = 9\text{ cm}$, and the non-included angle $A = 30^\circ$ (opposite side $a$). The height from the given angle is $h = b\sin A = 9\sin 30^\circ$. Determine how many distinct triangles satisfy these conditions, and justify using $h$.
items.answer: Two distinct triangles (the ambiguous SSA case).

steps: This is the SSA ambiguous case: two sides and a non-included angle.
Compute the height: $h = 9\sin 30^\circ = 9 \times \frac{1}{2} = 4.5\text{ cm}$.
Compare the opposite side $a = 6$ to $h$ and to $b$: since $h = 4.5 < a = 6 < b = 9$, the side $a$ is long enough to reach the base but shorter than $b$.
When $h < a < b$, the swinging side crosses the base in two places, so two non-congruent triangles satisfy the conditions.
Therefore there are two distinct triangles.

items.prompt: A set of conditions gives two angles of $35^\circ$ and $35^\circ$ and the included side of $8\text{ cm}$ between them. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one, or none? Name the criterion and find the third angle.
items.answer: Unique triangle by ASA; third angle $= 110^\circ$.

steps: Two angles with the side between them is the Angle-Side-Angle (ASA) configuration.
ASA fixes the triangle completely, so the triangle is unique up to congruence.
Find the third angle: $180^\circ - 35^\circ - 35^\circ = 110^\circ$.
The triangle is unique by ASA, with angles $35^\circ$, $35^\circ$, $110^\circ$.

items.prompt: The longest side of a triangle is $15\text{ cm}$. One other side is $9\text{ cm}$. Find the range of possible lengths for the remaining side $x$, given that $15$ must stay the longest side.
items.answer: $6\text{ cm} < x \le 15\text{ cm}$ (and combined with staying the longest side, $6\text{ cm} < x \le 15\text{ cm}$).

steps: Triangle inequality with sides $9$, $15$, and $x$: the two shorter sides must sum to more than the longest. Treating $15$ as longest, $9 + x > 15$, so $x > 6$.
For $15$ to remain the longest side, $x \le 15$.
Also check the other inequality $x + 15 > 9$, which holds for all positive $x$.
Combining: $6\text{ cm} < x \le 15\text{ cm}$.

items.prompt: Given sides $a = 5\text{ cm}$, $b = 8\text{ cm}$, and non-included angle $A = 90^\circ$ opposite $a$. How many triangles are possible? Justify.

steps: In any triangle the largest angle lies opposite the longest side.
Here the right angle $A = 90^\circ$ is given opposite side $a = 5$, but side $b = 8$ is longer than $a$.
The side opposite a $90^\circ$ angle (the hypotenuse) must be the longest side, yet $a = 5 < b = 8$, a contradiction.
No triangle can satisfy these conditions, so there are zero triangles.

items.prompt: A triangle has angles in the ratio $2 : 3 : 4$. Find all three angle measures, then state whether the conditions (only the ratio is given) determine a unique triangle, more than one, or none.
items.answer: Angles $40^\circ$, $60^\circ$, $80^\circ$; more than one triangle (AAA, infinitely many similar triangles).

steps: Let the angles be $2k$, $3k$, and $4k$. They sum to $180^\circ$: $2k + 3k + 4k = 9k = 180^\circ$.
Solve: $k = 20^\circ$.
The angles are $2k = 40^\circ$, $3k = 60^\circ$, $4k = 80^\circ$.
Only the three angles are fixed (AAA) and no side length is given, so the shape is determined but the size is not.
There are infinitely many similar triangles, so this gives more than one triangle.

items.prompt: For sides $a = 3\text{ cm}$, $b = 7\text{ cm}$ and non-included angle $A = 30^\circ$ opposite $a$, the height is $h = b\sin A = 7\sin 30^\circ = 3.5\text{ cm}$. Compare $a$ with $h$ to decide how many triangles are possible.

steps: SSA ambiguous-case test: compute the height $h = 7\sin 30^\circ = 7 \times \frac{1}{2} = 3.5\text{ cm}$.
Compare the opposite side $a = 3$ with $h = 3.5$: since $a = 3 < h = 3.5$, the side is too short to reach the base.
When the side opposite the given angle is shorter than the height, the swinging side never meets the base.
Therefore no triangle can be formed, so there are zero triangles.

items.prompt: An isosceles triangle has a vertex angle of $96^\circ$. Find each base angle, and explain why a vertex angle of $96^\circ$ is geometrically possible while a vertex angle of $180^\circ$ is not.

steps: In an isosceles triangle the two base angles are equal; call each $x$.
Angle sum: $96^\circ + x + x = 180^\circ$, so $2x = 84^\circ$ and $x = 42^\circ$.
Each base angle is $42^\circ$, and $96^\circ + 42^\circ + 42^\circ = 180^\circ$ checks out.
A vertex angle of $180^\circ$ would leave $0^\circ$ for the two base angles, collapsing the figure into a straight line, so it cannot form a triangle.

items.prompt: Two sides of a triangle are $12\text{ cm}$ and $5\text{ cm}$. List all whole-number lengths the third side could have.

steps: The third side $c$ must satisfy $|12 - 5| < c < 12 + 5$, that is $7 < c < 17$.
The whole numbers strictly between $7$ and $17$ are $8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16$.
Each of these gives a valid triangle, so there are $9$ possible whole-number lengths.

items.prompt: A triangle is described by sides $3\text{ cm}$ and $4\text{ cm}$ with an included right angle of $90^\circ$. Is the triangle unique? Name the criterion and find the length of the third side.
items.answer: Unique by SAS; the third side is $5\text{ cm}$.

steps: Two sides with the angle between them is the Side-Angle-Side (SAS) configuration, which determines a unique triangle.
The included angle is $90^\circ$, so the third side is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs $3$ and $4$.
By the Pythagorean theorem, $c = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5\text{ cm}$.
The triangle is unique by SAS, with third side $5\text{ cm}$.

items.prompt: Conditions: angle $A = 40^\circ$, angle $B = 75^\circ$, and the side opposite $A$ is $a = 6\text{ cm}$. First decide whether the third angle can be found, then classify whether the triangle is unique. Name the criterion.
items.answer: Third angle $C = 65^\circ$; unique triangle by AAS.

steps: Find the third angle: $C = 180^\circ - 40^\circ - 75^\circ = 65^\circ$.
Now two angles and a side opposite one of them are known, which is the Angle-Angle-Side (AAS) configuration.
AAS determines a unique triangle up to congruence (once two angles are known, all three are, and one fixed side sets the size).
The triangle is unique by AAS with $C = 65^\circ$.

items.prompt: A student claims that sides $6\text{ cm}$, $6\text{ cm}$, and $12\text{ cm}$ form a valid triangle because '$6 + 6 = 12$ is big enough.' Explain whether the student is correct and describe the resulting figure.
items.answer: Incorrect; no triangle forms. The figure collapses into a straight $12\text{ cm}$ segment.

steps: The triangle inequality requires the two shorter sides to sum to strictly more than the longest side: $6 + 6 > 12$ must be a strict inequality.
Here $6 + 6 = 12$, which is equal, not greater.
When the sum equals the longest side, the two shorter sides lie flat along the longest side, forming a degenerate triangle.
The figure collapses into a straight segment of length $12\text{ cm}$, so the student is incorrect and no triangle exists.

items.prompt: Given sides $a = 9\text{ cm}$ and $b = 6\text{ cm}$ with non-included angle $A = 50^\circ$ opposite the longer side $a$. Determine how many triangles are possible, and justify why the count differs from a typical ambiguous case.

steps: This is an SSA setup with the given angle opposite side $a$.
The given angle $A = 50^\circ$ is opposite $a = 9$, the longer of the two sides ($a > b$).
When the side opposite the given angle is longer than the other given side, the swinging side can only meet the base once.
So the ambiguity disappears: there is exactly one triangle. (The two-triangle case requires the opposite side to be shorter than the other side.)

items.prompt: A right trapezoid is to be drawn with two right angles, one pair of parallel sides of lengths $10\text{ cm}$ and $6\text{ cm}$, and a height of $4\text{ cm}$ between the parallel sides. Find the length of the slanted (non-perpendicular) side, and explain why these conditions determine a unique figure.
items.answer: The slanted side is $\sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}$; the conditions determine a unique right trapezoid.

steps: Place the two parallel sides ($10\text{ cm}$ and $6\text{ cm}$) with the height $4\text{ cm}$ perpendicular between them; the two right angles fix one vertical side as the height.
The horizontal offset of the slanted side equals the difference of the parallel sides: $10 - 6 = 4\text{ cm}$.
The slanted side is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs $4\text{ cm}$ (offset) and $4\text{ cm}$ (height): $\sqrt{4^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{16 + 16} = \sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}$.
Every measurement (both parallel sides, height, and the two right angles) is fixed, so only one trapezoid fits, making the figure unique.
